name: Gimi (Eastern Highlands)
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: McBride, Sam & Wendy McBride 1973. Notes on the essential features of the Gimi language, Eastern Highlands (SIL, Ukarumpa)

new_statements.quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress tends to occur on the first syllable carrying high pitch. The only tone contrast is between level tone and falling tone on the final vowel. ak 'seed' nimi 'bird' ák 'armband' nimí 'louse'
new_statements.citation: SIL PNG Branch. n.d. [printed 23 August 2004]. Gimi Organised Phonology Data. Manuscript, 3 pp. Ukarumpa: SIL (SIL Language & Culture Archives, entry 42483; draft posted without peer review; based on manuscripts by Sam McBride, Nancy Knippel, Jean Smith and J.A. Lloyd, 1965-1979).
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Gimi is described as having a word-level tone contrast (level vs falling tone on the final vowel of the word); stress is not independent of pitch but is reported to fall on the first syllable of the word that carries high pitch, i.e. it is pitch-conditioned rather than positionally fixed. Scott 1978:22 fn. 32 likewise reports (second-hand, from McBride & McBride 1973:15b) that Gimi is 'recorded as tonal'.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the statement is hedged ('tends to') and the data sheet is marked 'partly checked' and 'Draft (posted as is without peer review)'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (OPD lists tone on 'the final vowel' of the word and stress by syllable within the word); examples are isolated citation forms; no phrase-level statement.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD covers Gimi [gim] of Okapa district (villages Agipu, Urap, Negebi, Ubai), i.e. gimi1243 as a whole, with no dialect named. Haiman 1980 (not opened) describes the Zavina dialect (Zavina village) specifically; Glottolog lists no separate glottocode for Zavina. Glottolog's 'Wendy McBride' appears to be an error for Nancy McBride (Scott 1978:205 and the OPD bibliography).

The only tone contrast is between level tone and falling tone on the final vowel.' Examples ak 'seed' vs ák 'armband', nimi 'bird' vs nimí 'louse'. sources.citation: Wurm, Stephen A. 1975. Eastern Central Trans-New Guinea Phylum languages. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea Area Languages and Language Study Vol. 1: Papuan languages and the New Guinea linguistic scene, 461-526. Pacific Linguistics C-38. Canberra: ANU. (Glottolog 9720.)
sources.note: Family-level only, p. 477: 'In their phonologies, the East-Central Family languages show a strong development of supra-segmental features manifesting themselves in tonal systems and combined tone-stress systems. The glottal stop phoneme appears with extremely high statistical frequency in the languages of the Gahuku and the Kamano Sub-Families, and in Gimi.' Nothing Gimi-specific on stress placement.

sources.note: Metadata only; gives the PDF link used above.
Paraphrases the SIL OPD (cites archive 42483): tone section only ('The final vowel of a word takes either a level or falling tone'); no stress statement.

sources.citation: Scott, Graham. 1978. The Fore Language of Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics B-47. Canberra: ANU. (Glottolog 323312 = ch. 'Proto-Phonology', pp. 163-197.)
sources.note: About Gimi only second-hand: p. 22 fn. 32 'Languages recorded as tonal include Siane (Lucht and James 1962:13); Gahuku (Deibler 1976:5); Gimi (McBride and McBride 1973:15b). Those analysed as stress-based include Benabena..., Kamano..., Yagaria...'. The Proto-Phonology chapter uses Gimi cognates but says nothing about Gimi stress. Bibliography p. 205 lists McBride & McBride 1968 Survey Word List: Gimi; 1972 Gimi Grammar Essentials (typescript 66 pp); 1973 Gimi Phonemes (typescript 19 pp), Ukarumpa: SIL.
